items.title: Holman Bill — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Pete was never really a jazz writer.

ctx.x: Some other names: Pete Rugalo, Billy May.

No, they were up here. They were the guys that were getting all the work. Billy May was – he was doing an album a week and had the weekend to get sober again. He was – all those guys were in a different category. Pete was never really a jazz writer. His training was all classical. He managed to find a way that worked with Stan, worked very well, because that was – as far as I know, that was Stan‟s ideal. No, I take it back. Graettinger was Stan‟s ideal. In fact, there are rumors going around that all this other…

You say that you really got the arranging bug and you got your early training at Westlake College. Could you tell us a little bit more about the longevity of that institution? How long had it existed before you attended? How long did it last? How was it supported? Obviously, through tuition, since it was so expensive. Ate up your GI Bill.

items.title: Bill Holman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 13, 1999
items.q: Well the late 40s, the thing Rugulo was selling. I liked those a lot at the time.

ctx.x: He certainly generates discussion about where he fits in jazz history. How do you feel about his place?

Well there’s a definite place there. I don’t know, not being a historian it would be hard to say where it fits but he did a lot of things, he gave opportunities to a whole lot of people that were able to go on their own and have good careers. A lot of his music, well I liked very much. Well the late 40s, the thing Rugulo was selling. I liked those a lot at the time. Then later in the 50s, when I was into it I liked more swinging things. So that’s why I wasn’t able to write for him for a while, because I didn’t…
It sounds like right up his alley.
